newsitem.title: USA: Georgia GSP seen growing at 3.3 percent in 1997.
newsitem.headline: Georgia GSP seen growing at 3.3 percent in 1997.

text.p: Georgia's gross state product is expected to grow by 3.3 percent in 1997, down from five percent this year, University of Georgia economists said in their annual forecast.
The report, released Thursday, said the decline in growth would be a consequence of the economic boost the state
received from hosting the Olympic Games last summer.
Despite the slowdown, growth in Georgia's gross state product will outstrip the anticipated 2.2 percent growth in the nation's gross domestic product, the economists said.

The strongest gains for Georgia were anticipated in services, particularly in wholesale and retail trade. Other above average sectors will be transportation, communications and public utilities, the report said.

Industries that will suffer are textiles and apparel, both of which have been declining for many years due to automation and more recently NAFTA as companies shift jobs to Mexico. The state is expected to add 78,600 jobs in 1997, a 2.2 percent gain compared to the 3.7 percent advance in 1996.

J. Don Edwards, interim dean of the university's business school, said the job gains would be in line with the expected decline in the gross state product growth. He said Georgia's unemployment rate would remain below five percent.
The report said the 20-county metropolitan Atlanta area
would continue to drive the state's economy, accounting for 49,700, or 63 percent, of Georgia's new jobs.
Georgians' personal income was forecast to grow by three percent, nearly double the 1.6 percent forecast for the nation.
As strong in-migration continues, Georgia's population was expected to reach 7.5 million in July, an increase of two percent over July of 1996.

The report said construction activity would remain about the same as the cyclical high reached last year, with new housing units declining 0.4 percent. Single-family housing will experience a 1.6 percent increase as the multi-unit sector declines, the economists predicted. State revenues grew by 8.4 percent in fiscal 1996, which ended June 30. That growth should slow to 6.1 percent in the current fiscal year, the report said. The substantially lower growth reflects the slowing economy and an expected $187.5 million drop in state sales tax receipts.
Georgia repealed half of the four percent sales tax on groceries as of Oct 1. The remaining two percent is to be phased out in the next two years.
In fiscal 1998, revenue collections were forecast to rise by four percent, compared with 5.7 percent if the sales tax on food had remained in effect.

The major stimulus for Georgia's continuing to outpace the nation in economic growth is its low cost structure, which attracts companies to move to the state and encourages existing businesses to expand, the report said.

Down the road, the state will face problems with growth outstripping its infrastructure, the report said, citing already crowded roads and schools, aging bridges and limits on water distrubution and treatment. --Miami Bureau, 305-374-5013
